title: Look under your own collar
hookLine: if you are wise, don't write black marks against others; look within your own collar (Farid salok, ang 1378)

lines: A LEDGER OF OTHER PEOPLE'S MISTAKES.
cards: A red pen is a satisfying thing to hold. Circle the typo. Strike the wrong figure.
Some minds are very good at this, and not only with paper: they keep a running ledger of other people's mistakes, neat and up to date. Farid has a couplet for the person holding that pen.
We touched it earlier this year, when his verses came into the Guru's keeping. Today we stay with it, because it ends the week.

teach.b: On Ang 1378, in paraphrase: Farid, if you have a keen and subtle mind, don't write black marks against anyone else. Bow your head and look within your own collar. Three things are packed in.

First, who it's addressed to: not the fool, the clever one. Some readers hear in this that sharpness is exactly what makes a person good at spotting other people's faults. The gift and the danger are the same tool.
Second, the black marks. The picture is an account book, a record kept against someone. Farid doesn't say the faults aren't real.
He says don't be the one keeping the book. Third, the collar, the opening of a shirt at the neck.

teach.h: BOW TO SEE INSIDE YOUR COLLAR.
teach.b: To see inside it, you have to bow your head, the posture of prayer Farid called himself to at dawn. So looking at yourself honestly and bowing turn out to be one movement. And this whole week has circled that idea.

Kabir spoke his hymns to Loi, at home, where words have to be true. He went to Maghar, because the place doesn't save you. His saloks were short and sharp; he was blunt with pride and humble before everyone else.
Then Farid, rising to pray and admitting the way is hard, asking that the heart and the lips agree.

teach.h: A WEEK OF TURNING THE EYES INWARD.
teach.b: Every one turns the eyes inward.
The collar is the plainest picture of all: before the red pen moves, the head bows.

how: Farid's saloks are read and sung in gurdwaras with the rest of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs read this couplet as a reminder to examine oneself before judging others.

o: a leash for the ego, held tight in the Guru's hand
the badge of rank a court official wore at the neck
the neck of a shirt, where Farid says to bow and look first

games.q: inside the couplet — tap the pairs.
p: who the couplet is addressed to

s: Farid says other people's faults aren't real
he doesn't deny them; he says don't be the one keeping the book.
the couplet is addressed to the clever one
if you have a keen and subtle mind, don't write black marks against others.

games.q: you've spotted a colleague's mistake, and you're good at spotting them. Farid has addressed his couplet to you. what does it ask?
o: write it down so it isn't forgotten.
point it out to everyone, for fairness.
bow your head and look within your own collar.
games.why: Farid tells the clever mind not to write black marks against others, but to bow and look within its own collar.

practice: Let someone you've been marking come to mind, at work, online, at home, and notice the fault you've written down for them.
Then bow your head a little, really bow, and ask one plain question: where does that same thing show up in me? Don't rush the answer; if you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Collar. The opening of a shirt at the neck, where Farid tells the clever mind to bow and look, instead of writing black marks against anyone else.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: the collar, the opening at the neck where Farid says to look.

carryVoice: Your line: look within your collar. The clever eye works best turned inward. That's the week.
